Multi-Commodity Flow.definition: Model each resource type as a separate flow on the same network; balances multiple commodities simultaneously.
Multi-Commodity Flow.condition: Applies when the problem description involves multiple resource types that share a common network topology or capacities and interact through shared arcs or nodes.

Capacity/Resource Balance Equations.definition: Conserve each resource at every node: inflow - outflow = demand or supply.
Capacity/Resource Balance Equations.condition: Applies when the problem domain requires resources to move or transform through nodes and local conservation must hold.

Set-Partitioning/Assignment.definition: Assign each task to exactly one resource or agent using ∑_j x_ij = 1 constraints.
Set-Partitioning/Assignment.condition: Applies when the problem description requires each item or task to be exclusively assigned to exactly one choice among many.

Resource Pooling.definition: Aggregate interchangeable resources into a single pool before allocation.
Resource Pooling.condition: Applies when the problem domain contains multiple identical resources that are substitutable and individual identities do not matter.

Resource Ratio Coupling.definition: Couple two resource pools via a scalar automation ratio: number of concurrently active vehicles ≤ ratio × number of active operators.
Resource Ratio Coupling.condition: Applies when a human or automated supervisor can monitor and control multiple vehicles simultaneously, and the fleet activation is gated by available operator count multiplied by an automation factor.

Resource Ratio Coupling (Automation-Clas.definition: Fleet activation bounded by sum over automation classes of (class-specific ratio × pilots in that class).
Resource Ratio Coupling (Automation-Clas.condition: When remote pilot automation categories (HWTL, HOTL, HOVTL) each permit a distinct maximum vehicle-to-pilot ratio and pilots are assigned to those categories.

Eligibility-Constrained Assignment.definition: Assignment variable x_{i,j} exists only for eligible (task i, resource j) pairs; for ineligible pairs, variable is omitted or fixed to zero.
Eligibility-Constrained Assignment.condition: When regulatory or operational categories make some resources unsuitable for certain tasks, e.g., specific vehicle types for missions over people.

Multi-Resource Crew Bundle.definition: Each active vehicle of a special mission type simultaneously consumes fixed quantities of several distinct resource types; the allowed fleet size is bounded by the minimum resource availability across all required types.
Multi-Resource Crew Bundle.condition: When a mission type (e.g., medevac) demands a fixed multi‑role crew complement per vehicle, and each role is a separately limited resource pool, the number of active vehicles is capped by each pool’s capacity.

Concurrent Task Limit (Fixed Cardinality.definition: At most \(N\) simultaneous tasks of a given type can be executed at a facility, representing a known finite number of dedicated service points.
Concurrent Task Limit (Fixed Cardinality.condition: When a facility has a fixed, small number of identical resources (e.g., high‑voltage fast chargers, maintenance bays) that limit how many vehicles can perform that activity at the same time.

Cycle-Time Derived Service Capacity.definition: Limit the number of tasks per resource per day based on the resource’s cycle time (service + recharge), not just an arbitrary cap.
Cycle-Time Derived Service Capacity.condition: When a resource (pad) requires a fixed recharge or turnaround time after each use, and the total daily operational window is limited.

Coverage Slack Variables.definition: Introduce continuous slack variables to absorb unmet demand when total supply is insufficient, and penalize them in the objective.
Coverage Slack Variables.condition: When demand may exceed available resource capacity and partial under-coverage is allowed, but unmet demand should be minimized.

Polymatroid Joint Capacity.definition: Model joint capacity limits with a nondecreasing submodular set function f(S) that bounds the total resource used by any subset S; integral solutions for linear objectives.
Polymatroid Joint Capacity.condition: Applies when shared capacity among resources is described by a submodular function, not additive per‑resource caps.

Dual-Variable Slot Pricing.definition: Use optimal dual values of capacity constraints as prices for shared resources, balancing supply and demand economically.
Dual-Variable Slot Pricing.condition: Applies when a model allocates shared capacity among multiple users and a market‑based pricing mechanism is desired or used to guide payments.

Lifetime-Window Availability Summation.definition: Total available capacity in period t = sum of capacity additions over the preceding lifetime L periods.
Lifetime-Window Availability Summation.condition: Applies when resources have a fixed finite lifetime after which they become unavailable, and capacity is additive.

Proportional Resource Cap.definition: Limit one resource type's total quantity to at most a fraction φ of the sum of all resource types used.
Proportional Resource Cap.condition: When a regulatory or policy constraint caps a particular resource type (e.g., nuclear) to a maximum percentage of total capacity.

Dual Subgradient Capacity Pricing.definition: At breakpoints of the optimal cost function F(b) with respect to RHS b, multiple optimal dual solutions exist; each is a subgradient p satisfying F(b*) + p'(b−b*) ≤ F(b). Use the range of dual values as the marginal-cost interval for capacity pricing.
Dual Subgradient Capacity Pricing.condition: When using dual values for marginal cost pricing of shared resources (vertiport slots, airspace capacity) and the LP exhibits primal degeneracy or F(b) has a kink. Exclude when the LP has a unique nondegenerate dual solution (smooth F).
Dual Subgradient Capacity Pricing.explanation: The optimal cost F(b) of an LP is convex and piecewise-linear in RHS b. Where F is differentiable, the unique dual solution equals ∇F. At a breakpoint (primal degeneracy), multiple dual solutions exist, each a subgradient. The interval [p_min, p_max] of optimal dual values gives the range of valid marginal costs. Capacity pricing should use this interval, not a single dual value, to avoid underestimating resource value.
Dual Subgradient Capacity Pricing.example: Vertiport slot capacity b has dual value 45 in one optimal basis and 60 in another—both are valid subgradients. The true marginal value of one more slot lies in [45, 60]. For dynamic slot pricing, bid floors should use p_min to guarantee non-negative surplus; allocation prices should use p_max to reflect full opportunity cost. At breakpoints, small b changes may produce zero marginal change (p_min=0).

Revenue-Reinvestment Capacity Coupling.definition: The available capacity of a shared resource in period \(t\) is a fraction of the revenue earned in period \(t-1\), creating a dynamic link between sales and production decisions.
Revenue-Reinvestment Capacity Coupling.condition: Applies when operational capacity (cash, material) is replenished by reinvesting a fixed percentage of sales revenue from the immediately preceding period, typical in self-financed production systems.

Leontief Input-Output Productivity Verif.definition: Verify that the technology matrix A is productive before solving input-output models to guarantee nonnegative output for any nonnegative final demand.
Leontief Input-Output Productivity Verif.condition: Applies when modeling inter-sector flows where each sector consumes outputs of others in fixed proportions.

Dual-Sensitivity Bottleneck Expansion.definition: After solving an LP, compute dual values and allowable right-hand-side (RHS) ranges for each resource constraint; expand the resource with highest dual value whose allowable increase is positive.
Dual-Sensitivity Bottleneck Expansion.condition: Applies when capacity expansion decisions follow a production LP; the objective is revenue or profit, constraints are resource limits, and dual values indicate marginal value of relaxing each constraint.

Slack/Excess Balancing with Inter-Class.definition: Model flexible reallocation of a fixed total resource among classes by introducing nonnegative slack and excess variables per class, enforcing that the sum of excesses equals the sum of slacks (conservation), and capping each deviation.
Slack/Excess Balancing with Inter-Class.condition: When a fixed-capacity shared resource can be shifted between categories (e.g., seat classes, vehicle types) but per‑category adjustment is limited to a fraction, and total allocated must remain constant.

Battery Weight-Payload Coupling.definition: Couple battery capacity B (kWh) with available payload P via P = P_max − w·B, where w is the drone‑specific weight per kWh. This captures the drone design trade‑off between endurance and carrying capacity.
Battery Weight-Payload Coupling.condition: When the drone’s battery capacity is a decision variable (e.g., fleet design or mission‑specific sizing) and a larger battery physically reduces the maximum payload due to increased drone empty weight.

Multi-Stage Serial Power Allocation.definition: Allocate a shared power budget among sequential relay nodes, where each node's transmission power contributes to the SINR at the next hop, creating a chain of interdependent nonlinear constraints.
Multi-Stage Serial Power Allocation.condition: When a communication relay chain consists of multiple UAVs, and the end-to-end signal quality requires each hop's SINR to exceed a threshold, with a total power budget.

Fairness-Acceptance Pricing Penalty.definition: Dynamic pricing shifts spatio-temporal demand but incurs a dissatisfaction penalty modeled as a convex function of the price deviation from a reference (expected) price, capturing consumer fairness concerns.
Fairness-Acceptance Pricing Penalty.condition: When demand can be shifted via pricing but large price deviations cause backlash; model dissatisfaction as a penalty term in the objective that grows with the gap between offered and reference price.

Repositioning Flow Variables.definition: Introduce separate flow variables on network arcs for empty vehicle moves that rebalance supply to meet asymmetric demand; conserve flow with service variables.
Repositioning Flow Variables.condition: When vehicles must be relocated empty to match demand geographically and repositioning incurs cost/time; exclude when demand is symmetric or vehicles do not reposition.

Battery Thermal-Cooling Trade-off Constr.definition: Enforce a maximum safe battery temperature by linking discharge current, ambient conditions, and cooling system capacity, where cooling capacity introduces a weight penalty that reduces available payload or increases energy consumption.
Battery Thermal-Cooling Trade-off Constr.condition: When UAV battery thermal limits constrain high‑power operations and cooling can be added at the expense of extra mass.

Mutually Exclusive Technology Alternativ.definition: For each renewable unit (UAV, charger), select exactly one technology alternative via binary y_k; each alternative k carries its own fixed cost, emission factor, energy density, weight‑to‑capacity ratio, etc. Operational constraints and objective terms use those parameters weighted by the selection variables.
Mutually Exclusive Technology Alternativ.condition: When the design space includes distinct technology options (e.g., Li‑ion battery vs. hydrogen fuel cell) and the choice of technology alters multiple numeric coefficients throughout the model—not just a single cost parameter.
Mutually Exclusive Technology Alternativ.explanation: Introduce binary variables tech_i,t ∈ {0,1} with Σ_t tech_i,t = 1. Linked operational variables (battery capacity, energy consumption per km, payload limit, embodied emission) are expressed as Σ_t parameter_t * tech_i,t. This avoids duplicating all constraints per technology and makes the model compact while capturing the trade‑off between energy density, emission factor, and cost.
Mutually Exclusive Technology Alternativ.example: For each UAV, define binary tech_bat, tech_fc. Total emission = Σ_i (E_bat * tech_bat_i + E_fc * tech_fc_i) + Σ_i Σ_h cef[h] * p_ch_i[h] * tech_bat_i. Max payload = Σ_i (Pmax_bat * tech_bat_i + Pmax_fc * tech_fc_i). Energy consumed per km = Σ_i (e_bat * tech_bat_i + e_fc * tech_fc_i).

Queueing Fleet Size Constraint.definition: Derive the required fleet size as the sum of expected queue length at each open facility (from a queueing model) plus the total in-flight vehicle-time of all scheduled flights, converting queue length to fleet count via appropriate time scaling.
Queueing Fleet Size Constraint.condition: When fleet size is a decision variable and the system's service level or waiting time requirement imposes a limit on queue length; exclude when queueing is irrelevant or fleet size is fixed.

Time-Window Spill Limit.definition: Enforce that at most a given fraction of demand from each OD pair experiences total journey time exceeding a maximum allowed time; unmet demand beyond the limit must be rejected or penalized.

Closed Queueing Fleet Size Constraint.definition: Approximate a closed queueing network with linear constraints that sum average vehicle counts (via throughput and mean delay) plus in-transit vehicles to equal total fleet N, using Adelman's (2007) method to keep the formulation linear.
Closed Queueing Fleet Size Constraint.condition: When the system is a closed queueing network with finite vehicles (e.g., fleet size N fixed) and queueing delays are significant, the fleet balance must be enforced in an MIP without nonlinear queueing formulas.

Unimodal Profit-Driven Pricing.definition: When service price per unit is a decision variable and demand volume or acceptance probability is a decreasing function of total user cost, the profit objective (price−cost)×demand is typically unimodal with an interior optimum, which can be resolved via univariate subproblem or embedded via piecewise‑linear price‑response curves.
Unimodal Profit-Driven Pricing.condition: Demand depends on price (not fixed); unit cost is constant; profit is maximization over price.

Inventory Balance Equations.definition: Track stock level over time: I_t = I_{t-1} + production - demand.
Inventory Balance Equations.condition: Applies when the problem description involves materials or products that carry over between periods and must satisfy stock-flow balance.

Time-Indexed Variables.definition: Define decision variables for every period (e.g., x_t) to capture dynamics.
Time-Indexed Variables.condition: Applies when the problem domain requires discrete time modeling to capture capacities, setups, or carryover decisions.

Energy Balance Equations.definition: Track battery state of charge as a cumulative resource: E_t = E_{t-1} + charge_t - consumption_t, with lower and upper bounds.
Energy Balance Equations.condition: Applies when electric vehicles operate with limited battery capacity that can be replenished, and state of charge must remain within safe limits throughout a sequence of operations to prevent depletion or overcharging.

Facility‑Location Lot‑Sizing Formulation.definition: For uncapacitated lot sizing, use assignment variables w_{ik} ≤ x_j and Σ_j w_{jk}=1 where x_j is a setup binary; the LP relaxation yields integer w_{ik}, providing a tight convex hull.
Facility‑Location Lot‑Sizing Formulation.condition: When production setups are uncapacitated and demand occurs in discrete periods; extendable to multi‑item capacitated problems for strong LP bounds.

Alternative Bills-of-Materials Constrain.definition: When a product can be built using different components that consume distinct resources, duplicate the product variable for each alternative and impose separate capacity constraints for each resource.
Alternative Bills-of-Materials Constrain.condition: Applies when a product has multiple mutually substitutable input options (e.g., two memory board types) and each option consumes a different, limited resource; the product quantity can be split across variants.

Flow Conservation.definition: For each node: inflow - outflow = net demand (could be negative for supply).
Flow Conservation.condition: Applies when the problem description involves quantities traversing a directed network and nodal balance must be maintained.

Arc-Capacity Constraints.definition: Limit flow on each arc: 0 ≤ f_ij ≤ cap_ij.
Arc-Capacity Constraints.condition: Applies when the problem domain contains edges with maximum throughput or capacity limits.

Max-Flow Objective.definition: Maximize total flow sent from source to sink.
Max-Flow Objective.condition: Applies when the problem description requires maximizing throughput between designated source and sink nodes.

Multi-Commodity Flow.definition: Handle several flow types on shared arcs with coupling capacity.
Multi-Commodity Flow.condition: Applies when the problem domain contains distinct commodities that share arcs and compete for common capacities.

Time-Expanded Slot Network.definition: Model flows on a time-expanded network where both arcs (corridor segments) and nodes (vertiport pads) have finite per-period capacities using time-indexed binary occupancy variables.
Time-Expanded Slot Network.condition: Applies when vehicles/flights move through discretized space-time and both transit segments and terminal slots are capacity-constrained per time step.

Arc Activation Constraints.definition: Flow on an arc is allowed only when a binary activation variable equals 1, enforced via Big-M: flow_arc ≤ M × z_arc.
Arc Activation Constraints.condition: Applies when network arcs can be toggled open or closed by external conditions (weather, airspace restrictions, NOTAMs) and flow may only traverse active arcs.

Node Capacity Constraints.definition: Limit the total flow entering or leaving a node per time period to respect facility processing limits.
Node Capacity Constraints.condition: Applies when nodes represent facilities (vertiports, warehouses) that have finite throughput capacity per time step.

Geofence Arc Exclusion.definition: Arcs that intersect geofenced no-fly zones are removed from the network or have their upper capacity forced to zero, ensuring flows never traverse prohibited airspace.
Geofence Arc Exclusion.condition: When flight corridors or vehicle routes must respect static geofence polygons representing off-limits areas (e.g., airports, sensitive infrastructure).

Noise Budget Constraint.definition: Limit cumulative noise exposure from all flights over arcs crossing noise-sensitive areas to a regulatory threshold, where each arc has a known noise increment per flight.
Noise Budget Constraint.condition: When environmental regulation imposes an aggregate noise cap over a planning horizon, and flights may choose routes that traverse populated zones with quantifiable noise impact.

Layered Altitude Network Flow.definition: Represent airspace as a multi-layer directed graph where each layer contains horizontal arcs between fixed nodes, and vertical transition arcs connect layers at specific waypoints to allow altitude changes.
Layered Altitude Network Flow.condition: When the airspace can be stratified into distinct altitude bands with one-way corridors and aircraft may change altitude only at designated transition points.

Authorization-Gated Arc Activation.definition: Flow on an arc intersecting controlled airspace is permitted only if a binary authorization variable equals 1, enforced via Big-M; authorization may be deterministic or scenario-contingent.
Authorization-Gated Arc Activation.condition: When flight arcs cross airspace sectors governed by real-time authorization systems (LAANC, UTM) where each operation requires explicit regulatory approval before traversal.

Fluid Throughput Flow Approximation.definition: Treat high‑volume small‑package drone cargo flows as continuous variables (packages per hour) in a network flow model, using flow conservation and node throughput capacities to approximate discrete item movement.
Fluid Throughput Flow Approximation.condition: When cargo consists of many small items (≤5 lb each) and throughput is high enough (hundreds per hour), making individual package tracking unnecessary and continuous flow a valid approximation.

Noise Budget with Category Exclusions.definition: Cumulative noise budget constraint sums noise contributions only from non‑exempt flight categories, ignoring exempt missions like medevac.
Noise Budget with Category Exclusions.condition: When noise regulations exempt certain operations (emergency/medical) from counting toward community noise limits.

Angle-Difference Outer Subtraction for T.definition: Use column vector and outer subtraction to compute pairwise angle differences, then apply sin/cos in constraints via general function constraints, enabling vectorized flow equations.
Angle-Difference Outer Subtraction for T.condition: When modeling AC power flow or any flow network where branch constraints involve trigonometric functions of angle differences between nodes.

Dummy Node for Supply-Demand Imbalance.definition: Add a dummy sink with zero-cost arcs to absorb excess supply, or a dummy source with high-cost arcs to supply unmet demand, maintaining pure network structure.
Dummy Node for Supply-Demand Imbalance.condition: Applies when total supply and demand are not equal in a transportation/assignment/min-cost flow problem and the excess must be accounted for without forcing deliveries.

Node-Splitting for Arc Lower Bound Enfor.definition: Enforce a mandatory flow lower bound L on an arc by splitting the arc via an extra node, transforming the lower bound into capacity changes and node supply adjustments, keeping the problem as a pure min-cost network flow.
Node-Splitting for Arc Lower Bound Enfor.condition: Applies when an arc (i,j) has a positive lower bound L on flow and the model must remain a network flow (no explicit lower bound constraints). Excess flow beyond L is allowed up to capacity U.

Negative Cycle Detection for Unbounded M.definition: Before solving a shortest-path or min-cost flow problem where recirculation is possible, check for negative-cost cycles; their presence causes unboundedness (infinite negative net flow).
Negative Cycle Detection for Unbounded M.condition: Applies when arc costs can be negative and flows can circulate without capacity or when capacities are infinite; typical in pure shortest-path formulations without cycle elimination.

k-Connectivity Flow Constraints for Netw.definition: Enforce that the selected active arcs and nodes guarantee k edge- or node-disjoint paths between specified source-sink pairs, ensuring connectivity survives up to k-1 failures.
k-Connectivity Flow Constraints for Netw.condition: When the problem requires designing or selecting a subset of arcs/nodes (flight corridors, hubs) that must remain connected with alternative paths even under component failures, and the number of disjoint routes is a resilience requirement.

Hierarchical Layer Conflict Elimination.definition: Stratify airspace into disjoint altitude layers with directed one-way corridors in each layer; vertical transitions are restricted to designated waypoints. When flows are assigned to layers such that crossing traffic is eliminated, pairwise conflicts reduce to zero by structural design.
Hierarchical Layer Conflict Elimination.condition: When airspace can be vertically stratified into at least three altitude bands with unidirectional horizontal flows, and vehicles may change altitude only at fixed transition points; exclude when free-form 3D routing is required or vertical transitions are unbounded.

Flow-Dependent Arc Travel Cost (BPR).definition: Arc traversal cost is a non‑decreasing function of flow, typically c_a = t0*(1+α(f/C)^β). For system optimum, use marginal cost c + f*∂c/∂f.
Flow-Dependent Arc Travel Cost (BPR).condition: When UAV traffic along corridors is dense enough that congestion increases travel time or energy; flow‑dependent cost must be captured to model equilibrium.

Safety‑Density Derived Arc Capacity.definition: Arc capacity C_arc = ρ_max * v * w, where ρ_max is the maximum safe areal density (UAVs per m²), v is cruise speed, and w is the effective corridor width.
Safety‑Density Derived Arc Capacity.condition: When airspace safety regulations impose a minimum spatial separation between UAVs that translates to a maximum density, and corridor dimensions and speed are known.

Uniform-Boundary Continuum Reduction.definition: When a 2D continuum traffic model (flow conservation + density-dependent Eikonal equation) has uniform outflow density on the delivery boundary, the coupled PDE system reduces to a Poisson equation ∇²φ = constant with pure Neumann boundary conditions, yielding analytical or fast numerical solutions.
Uniform-Boundary Continuum Reduction.condition: When modeling high-density UAV traffic as a 2D continuum where delivery demand is uniformly distributed along the boundary. Exclude when outflow is non-uniform, exits are discrete and sparse, or individual vehicle trajectories must be tracked.

Continuum Flow-Potential Equilibrium Mod.definition: Represent UAV traffic in a 2D region as a continuum: a vector flux field f(x) and scalar cost potential u(x) satisfy the equilibrium condition (f/‖f‖)c(‖f‖)+∇u=0 and mass conservation ∇·f = source term, with boundary conditions. Solve via mixed finite elements.
Continuum Flow-Potential Equilibrium Mod.condition: When the airspace is densely populated with UAVs and traffic behaves as a fluid (high density, wide area), a continuum PDE model captures congestion propagation more faithfully than a sparse discrete network. Exclusion: when the domain has few distinct corridors and discrete flows dominate.

Continuum Density-to-Inflow Capacity Bou.definition: Translate a local maximum safe density ρ(x) ≤ ρ0 into a global bound on total inflow by integrating the mass conservation equation connecting inflow flux to density distribution.
Continuum Density-to-Inflow Capacity Bou.condition: When a safety regulation prescribes a maximum areal density of UAVs (e.g., 1 per 50 m²) and the traffic is modeled as a continuum. Not needed when each arc's density limit is enforced separately or when discrete corridor models provide explicit per-link capacities.

Visibility-Weighted Noise Metric.definition: Multiply noise emission per arc (dB) by the line-of-sight fraction to the exposed population, then sum or constrain the weighted product rather than raw dB.
Visibility-Weighted Noise Metric.condition: When noise externalities vary by corridor because some arcs are visible from populated areas while others are shielded by terrain or buildings; raw dB budgets ignore this spatial heterogeneity.

Ground Risk Threshold Arc Restriction.definition: An arc (corridor segment) over densely populated areas is prohibited or heavily penalized if the product of flight frequency and per-flight ground casualty risk exceeds a statutory safety threshold; precompute the risk product and set arc upper bound to zero where threshold is violated.
Ground Risk Threshold Arc Restriction.condition: When flight corridors traverse populated areas and regulatory safety targets (e.g., 10⁻⁶ fatalities per flight hour) impose absolute limits on aggregate ground risk. Exclude when ground risk is negligible or corridors avoid all populated areas.

Corridor Configuration Selection.definition: Select among predefined standard corridor configurations (one-way, with passing zones, multi-track) on each arc to trade off throughput and externalities.
Corridor Configuration Selection.condition: When designing flight corridors whose physical layout can be chosen from a small set of discrete standard designs, each offering a known maximum throughput and noise/externality per flight.

Joint Facility-Corridor Activation Coupl.definition: Link the opening of a facility (vertiport) with the availability of feasible flight corridors connecting it to the network via binary constraints, ensuring a facility is opened only if at least one feasible corridor incident to it exists, and a corridor arc is feasible only if both endpoint facilities are open.
Joint Facility-Corridor Activation Coupl.condition: When siting vertiports, each candidate site requires at least one flyable approach/departure corridor free of obstacles, and corridors may only be activated if both connected vertiports are opened. Use binary variables y_j for facility, z_{ij} for feasible corridor arc.

Schultz Curve DNL Noise Contour Constrai.definition: Model cumulative noise exposure at population centroids using the Schultz curve (DNL = L_E + 10·log₁₀(N) − 13.3 for N flights with single-event noise L_E); aggregate over hexagon grid cells and enforce DNL ≤ 65 dB as a linear constraint on flight frequency per arc.
Schultz Curve DNL Noise Contour Constrai.condition: When noise-sensitive vertiport/vertistop siting must respect regulatory DNL thresholds and flight paths can be mapped to hexagon cells with precomputed single-event noise exposure per arc–cell pair. Exclude when noise is not a binding constraint or a coarser noise metric suffices.

Utilisation-Tier Flow Assignment via Pre.definition: When node utilization levels affect demand capture, precompute maximum feasible flow per OD pair per utilization tier. Use binary variables to select a tier per node, and enforce actual flow equals a weighted combination of precomputed bounds plus a big-M term that forces zero flow if either endpoint is closed.
Utilisation-Tier Flow Assignment via Pre.condition: Applies when passenger demand is sensitive to service level (e.g., via logit) and the relationship between utilization and maximum capture can be evaluated offline; exclude when demand is static or continuous.

Service-Level-Dependent Arc Travel Time.definition: The effective travel time on a network arc is a function of the facility service level at the origin, modeled as a linear combination of flight time and ground-only time weighted by the service level parameter.
Service-Level-Dependent Arc Travel Time.condition: When a facility's service frequency or quality affects the total journey time for users, and service level is a decision variable.

Flow–Acceptance–Service Coupling.definition: Transit flow on an OD pair is expressed as ψ = (α * D) / (n * ρ), where α is passenger acceptance probability, D is total demand, n is number of service trips, and ρ is the service level.
Flow–Acceptance–Service Coupling.condition: When passenger acceptance depends on mode choice model and service level determines the number of flights per unit demand; used to ensure flow respects both customer acceptance and operational frequency.

Pricing–Fleet Co‑optimization Coupling.definition: Link the service price per unit, passenger acceptance, and fleet size via constraints that make acceptance decrease with price, and fleet size must satisfy total service trips derived from accepted demand.
Pricing–Fleet Co‑optimization Coupling.condition: Price is a decision variable, fleet size is integer, and acceptance is a decreasing function of price.
Pricing–Fleet Co‑optimization Coupling.explanation: Pricing affects accepted demand and thus vehicle trips needed; fleet cost influences profit, altering optimal price. Disjoint optimization yields suboptimal solutions. Model them jointly: include acceptance function α(p), fleet size Γ, and demand‑derived flow constraints.

Fixed Charge (Big-M Linking).definition: Open-close binary y_j with customer flow constrained by M·y_j.
Fixed Charge (Big-M Linking).condition: Applies when the problem description specifies that service or flow is allowed only if a facility is opened.

Customer Assignment Constraints.definition: Each customer assigned to exactly one open facility.
Customer Assignment Constraints.condition: Applies when the problem domain requires every demand point to be uniquely served by a single facility.

Multimodal Linkage Constraints.definition: Require that an opened facility must be reachable from demand points via ground transport within a given distance/time threshold, and assignment of demand to the facility is only allowed if the ground connection satisfies that threshold.
Multimodal Linkage Constraints.condition: Applies when a facility serves as a transshipment point between two modes (air and ground) and last-mile delivery feasibility is mandatory.

Logit Choice Demand Allocation.definition: Demand fraction assigned to a facility follows exp(utility) / sum exp(utility), where utility may depend on decision variables.
Logit Choice Demand Allocation.condition: When users choose among facilities probabilistically and the attractiveness of a facility is influenced by endogenous model decisions (e.g., location, congestion, service time).

Obstacle Clearance Surface Feasibility.definition: A vertiport site may only be opened if its ICAO/EASA obstacle limitation surfaces (approach, departure, transitional) are free of penetrating obstacles; enforced via a precomputed feasibility indicator or spatial constraints.
Obstacle Clearance Surface Feasibility.condition: Applies when locating vertiports/vertistops where candidate sites must respect 3D clearance surfaces to ensure safe takeoff/landing.

Capacity Envelope from Design Decisions.definition: Express the throughput capacity of a facility (vertiport) as a function of binary/multi‑level design decisions (pad count, layout type) via linear constraints, so capacity is endogenous rather than a fixed parameter.
Capacity Envelope from Design Decisions.condition: Applies when infrastructure capacity (e.g., landings per hour) is not given but directly determined by design choices (number of FATO stands, simultaneous/turn‑in‑hover operations) that are themselves decision variables.

Spatial Feasibility Mask.definition: Pre‑compute a binary feasibility indicator for each candidate site that aggregates multiple spatial constraints (obstacle clearance, building setbacks, geofences, roof area, wind feasibility, transit proximity) and exclude infeasible sites from the optimization model.
Spatial Feasibility Mask.condition: When candidate sites must satisfy multiple spatial constraints that can be evaluated offline using GIS layers; infeasible sites can be removed to shrink the binary variable set.

Attractiveness Score Aggregation.definition: Replace a detailed demand‑assignment model with a pre‑computed composite attractiveness score per candidate site, obtained by weighted sum of buffer‑based demographic counts; maximize total score of selected sites as objective.
Attractiveness Score Aggregation.condition: When the goal is to locate facilities to best serve spatially diffuse demand without needing exact demand point assignment, and multiple demand proxies influence attractiveness.

Threshold-Activated Logit Choice.definition: Demand switches to a new mode only if the disutility reduction (e.g., time savings) exceeds a minimum threshold; otherwise zero demand is assigned, creating a step function before logit allocation.
Threshold-Activated Logit Choice.condition: When mode shift requires a minimum perceptible benefit, such as time savings ≥ 25%, and users ignore small improvements, demand capture is zero below the threshold and follows a logit model above it.

Multi-Echelon Facility Role Assignment.definition: Ensure that flows follow a prescribed tier hierarchy: vehicles must travel from last‑mile stops through transfer ports to aggregation hubs and not bypass intermediate tiers, enforced by connectivity constraints and fixed facility types.
Multi-Echelon Facility Role Assignment.condition: When a multi‑echelon network requires distinct facility roles with flow passing through higher‑level nodes before reaching lower‑level destinations.

Capacity-Responsive Footprint Constraint.definition: Constrain the required area of a facility as a linear function of its designed throughput: Area ≥ base_area + α * throughput, where α is the additional area per unit movement per hour.
Capacity-Responsive Footprint Constraint.condition: When facility area is a design variable directly driven by the number of pads/taxiways needed to achieve a target hourly capacity, and empirical area‑per‑movement ratios are known.

Tiered Capacity Activation.definition: Select at most one discrete tier per facility site via binary variables; each tier unlocks a pre-defined capacity envelope (pads, chargers, gates) and incurs a tier-specific fixed cost, enforced via Big-M linking.
Tiered Capacity Activation.condition: When a facility can be opened at one of several discrete service tiers (vertipad, vertiport, vertihub) and each tier bundles a fixed maximum capacity and cost, rather than capacities being independently scalable.

Functional Area Budget Constraints.definition: Total facility site area must be at least the sum of minimum functional area allocations for package handling, charging stations, ground gates, and security, each scaling with throughput or fixed.
Functional Area Budget Constraints.condition: When a vertiport must accommodate multiple physical functions that compete for a limited total site area, and each function has a known minimum area requirement.

Range Feasibility Constraint.definition: Enforce that a route between two facilities may be used only if the distance does not exceed the vehicle’s maximum range; disallowed pairs are pre‑eliminated or forced to zero flow.
Range Feasibility Constraint.condition: When vehicle range (e.g., 150 miles for an eVTOL) limits which origin‑destination pairs can be served, and candidate routes/pairs are predefined. Exclude when range is not a binding limitation.

Remote Site Transit Extension Cost and T.definition: When a remote vertiport site is opened, it obligates construction of a transit link (e.g., people mover) with known travel time and monetary cost; passenger assignment to that site must then incur the extra travel time, and total door‑to‑door journey time must not exceed a maximum acceptable value.
Remote Site Transit Extension Cost and T.condition: Applies when candidate vertiport locations have heterogeneous ground access connectivity: some are directly connected to the terminal (zero extra time) while others require building a transit extension, incurring a fixed investment cost and a measurable travel time penalty.

Bilevel Incentive Location Design.definition: Model a Stackelberg game where a public leader offers per-site subsidies to influence a private follower's binary location decisions, with the follower maximizing profit minus cost given the subsidy.
Bilevel Incentive Location Design.condition: When a government or planner provides financial incentives to private operators to install infrastructure (e.g., vertiports) and the operator's opening decisions depend on the subsidy amounts.

Tier-Gated Service Eligibility.definition: Selecting a facility tier via binary variables determines which service types are permitted; eligibility constraints ensure a service variable can be active only if a chosen tier supports it.
Tier-Gated Service Eligibility.condition: When discrete infrastructure tiers (vertipad, vertiport, vertihub) imply mutually exclusive capabilities for service types.

Security-Triggered Fixed Cost.definition: Presence of a sterile area at a facility triggers a regulatory requirement (TSA security program) that incurs a fixed cost, modeled via a binary indicator coupled with a fixed charge.
Security-Triggered Fixed Cost.condition: When a design decision to include sterile zones for screened passengers activates mandatory regulatory compliance costs.

Equity Coverage Constraint.definition: Require that a minimum fraction of demand from a designated disadvantaged group is covered by at least one opened facility, ensuring equitable access.
Equity Coverage Constraint.condition: When policy or equity mandates that a protected population (e.g., displaced commuters, low‑income census tracts) receives a guaranteed level of service coverage, not just overall coverage.

Mandatory Opening via Regulation.definition: Fix the binary opening variable y_j = 1 for sites where building codes or other regulations mandate a facility, removing the site from the set of binary decisions and reducing variables.
Mandatory Opening via Regulation.condition: When regulations require that a facility of a certain type be present at a site, e.g., rooftop helipads mandated by building codes for structures over a height threshold.

Notice-Period Operational Delay.definition: Enforce a minimum lag of L time periods between a facility's approval/construction start and its operational availability, using constraints that link operational binary to past approval decisions.
Notice-Period Operational Delay.condition: When a newly established facility must wait a mandatory regulatory notice period (e.g., FAA Form 7460-1) before it can be used, and the model includes time phasing.

Altitude‑Dependent Facility Design.definition: The hover altitude h of an airborne fulfillment center is a continuous decision variable that influences drone energy consumption (ascent, descent, hover) and traffic density peak; trade‑off between delivery time and energy.
Altitude‑Dependent Facility Design.condition: When an airborne hub can operate at a variable height and the energy/speed profile of drones depends on altitude changes. Exclude when facility is fixed at ground level.

Altitude-Energy and Density Optimization.definition: When an airborne facility's hover height h is a continuous decision variable, model drone energy consumption as a function of altitude difference and gravitational potential, and enforce a peak drone density limit that depends on h.
Altitude-Energy and Density Optimization.condition: Applies when facility can operate at variable height and drone flights involve significant altitude changes; exclude when facility is fixed on ground or altitude has negligible energy impact.

Bilevel Network Design with Congestion E.definition: Upper-level problem selects discrete infrastructure arcs (guideways, corridors) under budget; lower-level problem solves user-equilibrium traffic assignment on the resulting network. Together this forms an MPEC or bilevel program that captures the planner's inability to control user route choices.
Bilevel Network Design with Congestion E.condition: When the planner can add or remove network arcs to relieve congestion and users route selfishly according to Wardrop equilibrium. Exclude when the planner controls both infrastructure and routing centrally (single-level SO), or when congestion is absent.

Landmark k‑Coverage for Localization.definition: Place a minimum‑cost set of visual landmarks (facilities) such that every grid cell in the environment is covered by at least k landmarks within line‑of‑sight range, enabling robust localization in GPS‑denied settings.
Landmark k‑Coverage for Localization.condition: When drones operate indoors or in urban canyons without GPS and rely on visual landmarks for pose estimation; each operating point must be continuously covered by at least k landmarks for redundancy.

3D Coverage Placement with Signal Propag.definition: Place aerial base stations at candidate 3D positions to maximize coverage of demand points, where coverage depends on line-of-sight and signal attenuation models, formulated as a maximum covering location problem.
3D Coverage Placement with Signal Propag.condition: When UAVs serve as aerial communication relays and the coverage area depends on altitude, obstacles, and propagation limits; excludes scenarios where coverage is a simple distance threshold without 3D constraints.

Facility Grid Capacity Coupling.definition: Jointly optimize facility location and the sizing of a supporting resource (e.g., electrical grid connection) that limits operational throughput and incurs a linear cost, with the resource capacity acting as a coupling constraint between location and scheduling decisions.
Facility Grid Capacity Coupling.condition: When opening a facility (vertiport) requires securing a finite, costly supporting resource whose capacity constrains the maximum simultaneous operational load, and the capacity can be chosen as a continuous or tiered design variable.

Multi‑Period Tiered Capacity with Monoto.definition: For each facility and period, select exactly one discrete capacity tier via binary variables; the tier index or resulting capacity level must be non‑decreasing over time to model staged, irreversible expansion.
Multi‑Period Tiered Capacity with Monoto.condition: Infrastructure capacity is built in discrete blocks (pad counts, charger racks) over multiple periods and cannot be reduced once installed. Exclude when capacity can be adjusted downward or is continuous.

Non‑Decreasing Capacity Constraint.definition: Enforce that a facility's nominal capacity in period t is at least its capacity in period t−1, preventing decommissioning of installed infrastructure.
Non‑Decreasing Capacity Constraint.condition: Multi‑period planning where capacity is irreversible; used for pads, gates, chargers that are permanently built. Exclude if capacity can be actively reduced or sold.

Altitude-Cap Range-Coverage Constraint.definition: When an altitude ceiling is imposed, the maximum horizontal distance a drone can cover without recharging is reduced due to climb/descent energy penalties; the distance between consecutive charging stations or the coverage radius of a station must be bounded by this altitude‑capped range.
Altitude-Cap Range-Coverage Constraint.condition: When planning charging station locations under airspace altitude limits that affect drone energy consumption per flight, and the range is sensitive to altitude changes.

Stochastic Demand-Scenario Facility Loca.definition: First stage selects facility locations under uncertain demand locations/magnitudes given as discrete scenarios with probabilities; second stage assigns demand per scenario, with coupling constraints that only open facilities can serve.
Stochastic Demand-Scenario Facility Loca.condition: When UAV charging stations must be placed to serve stochastically varying demand (e.g., on‑demand drone operations at random locations), and demand can be discretized into scenarios with known probabilities.

Gate-to-Pad Ratio Constraint.definition: Enforce a design ratio between the number of aircraft gates G and landing pads P, e.g., 2P ≤ G ≤ 8P, derived from empirical guidelines linking throughput and turnaround efficiency.
Gate-to-Pad Ratio Constraint.condition: When designing a vertiport, the count of gates (stands) must be bounded relative to the count of pads to avoid congestion or wasted footprint. Use as a structural constraint linking integer capacity variables G_i and P_i.

Queue-Derived Throughput Capacity.definition: Derive the maximum hourly throughput of a multi-pad vertiport from a queuing model (e.g., M/D/n with minimum time headway buffers) rather than assuming a fixed per-pad rate. The resulting capacity is a non‑linear function of the number of pads and the required separation; it is then embedded (often via piecewise-linear approximation) as an upper bound in location and network flow models.
Queue-Derived Throughput Capacity.condition: Applies when a facility’s (vertiport) throughput depends on stochastic arrival/departure processes and strict separation minima between vehicles, causing the total throughput to saturate sub‑linearly with the number of pads. Exclude when a simple fixed rate per pad is adequate or when separation effects are negligible.

Go-Around Loop Feasibility.definition: A candidate vertiport site is feasible only if a closed-loop go-around path exists from the landing decision point back to the landing direction point, remaining within the safe operating volume and free of obstacles.
Go-Around Loop Feasibility.condition: Applies when vertiport design mandates a go-around trajectory for balked landing, forming a continuous loop that must not exit the protected airspace; modeled as a pre-screening spatial check or a graph connectivity constraint.

Stochastic Simulation Capacity Inflation.definition: When deterministic pad‑count sizing ignores stochastic service times, inflate the deterministic plan by a factor derived from simulation with Poisson arrivals and lognormal pad occupancy, ensuring the designed capacity meets the target service level under uncertainty.
Stochastic Simulation Capacity Inflation.condition: Apply when pad occupancy times are lognormally distributed and arrivals are Poisson, and a deterministic model underestimates required pads. Exclude when a full stochastic queuing model (M/G/n) is already embedded in the optimization or when service times are deterministic.

Gate-Level Service Tier Assignment.definition: Assign a discrete service tier (e.g., short-turnaround/minimal services vs. long-turnaround/full charging+MRO) to each gate via binary variables, each tier carrying predetermined turnaround time, cost, and resource set.
Gate-Level Service Tier Assignment.condition: When designing a vertiport, gates can be configured with different service capabilities; the choice affects capacity, cost, and which vehicles can use them. Exclude if all gates are identical.

Closure as Zero-Tier Option.definition: Model facility closure as an explicit tier with zero capacity and zero fixed cost, unifying the open/close decision with tier selection. This avoids separate binary open variables and simplifies linking constraints via big‑M when closure must force zero flows.
Closure as Zero-Tier Option.condition: When a facility can be opened at one of several discrete capacity/service levels, and closure is equivalent to selecting a level with zero throughput and no cost; exclude if closure incurs a positive decommissioning cost or if levels are continuous.

Flow Conservation.definition: Vehicle enters and leaves each visited node once (or with load balance).
Flow Conservation.condition: Applies when the problem description requires feasible vehicle tours with balanced entry and exit at each visited node.

Set Partitioning/Assignment.definition: Each customer appears in exactly one route.
Set Partitioning/Assignment.condition: Applies when the problem domain requires every customer to be served exactly once across all vehicles.

Subtour Elimination Constraints.definition: Prevent cycles not containing the depot (e.g., MTZ, SEC).
Subtour Elimination Constraints.condition: Applies when the problem description allows decision variables to form disconnected cycles that must be eliminated.

Time-Windows Formulation.definition: Respect earliest/latest service times via arrival variables.
Time-Windows Formulation.condition: Applies when the problem domain specifies customer time windows or penalizes early/late service.

Cumulative Risk Constraint (Exposure Lim.definition: Sum of risk costs along a selected path must not exceed a safety threshold.
Cumulative Risk Constraint (Exposure Lim.condition: Applies when routes cross a risk map where each spatial arc/cell has a known risk value (e.g., fatality risk per flight) and total mission exposure must be bounded.

Sensor Coverage Feasibility Constraint.definition: A trajectory segment is permitted only if the vehicle's onboard sensor suite can detect obstacles within the required lookahead distance, given the segment's speed and the sensor's coverage radius/gate.
Sensor Coverage Feasibility Constraint.condition: Applies when vehicle autonomy relies on real-time obstacle detection and the sensing range is limited, requiring that the route never enters areas where detection distance is less than the safe stopping or avoidance distance.

Multimodal Ground Movement Choice.definition: For a required ground movement from pad to gate (or vice versa), select exactly one of several parallel alternative arcs representing different taxi modes, each with fixed travel time and energy consumption, enforced by sum_k x_{m,k} = 1.
Multimodal Ground Movement Choice.condition: Applies when a vehicle must taxi between two ground points and can choose among propulsion modes (hover, passive tow, active wheel) that have distinct speeds and energy draws, affecting schedule timing and battery state.

Headway-Augmented Edge Cost.definition: Increase edge traversal time by the minimum required time headway when the edge is already occupied, instead of enforcing separation via binary ordering constraints.
Headway-Augmented Edge Cost.condition: When vehicles sharing a directed segment must maintain a temporal gap, and a sequential planner can track edge occupancy.

Arc Time Propagation (Big-M).definition: Enforce arrival time consistency along a route by linking the time at node j to time at node i via travel plus service time, activated only when the arc is traversed by a vehicle: τ_j ≥ τ_i + service_i + travel_ij − M(1−δ_ij).
Arc Time Propagation (Big-M).condition: Applies when modeling vehicle routes with time windows and variable sequences, where the order is determined by binary arc-selection variables, not a fixed sequence.

Vehicle Rendezvous Synchronization Const.definition: Enforce that a drone is launched from a truck at a stop only after the truck arrives, and must return before truck departs or at a subsequent meeting point; track drone battery to ensure energy feasibility over the sortie.
Vehicle Rendezvous Synchronization Const.condition: When a truck serves as a mobile base for drones, and drone sorties must occur while the truck is stationary at a stop, with battery-limited range.

Mobile Arc-Based Drone Recovery Synchron.definition: Enforce that a drone launched from a truck can be retrieved while the truck is moving along an arc; the meeting point is parameterized by truck travel time fraction, and the drone's sortie duration must match that fraction, subject to battery and payload limits.
Mobile Arc-Based Drone Recovery Synchron.condition: When the truck acts as a mobile drone base and retrieval can occur anywhere along a route segment without requiring the truck to stop, increasing operational flexibility but combinatorial complexity.

Multi-Drop Drone Sortie Routing with Loa.definition: Model a drone's sortie as a vehicle routing problem with multiple customer visits per flight; track payload decreasing after each delivery and energy consumption accumulating with distance and current payload weight.
Multi-Drop Drone Sortie Routing with Loa.condition: When drones can carry multiple parcels and serve several customers before returning, and both payload capacity and battery endurance are binding.

Payload-Weighted Energy Consumption Cons.definition: For each flight arc, energy consumed increases linearly with payload mass carried on that arc: e_{arc} = α·distance + β·payload·distance, where α,β are constants.
Payload-Weighted Energy Consumption Cons.condition: When drone power draw depends significantly on carried weight, as with multirotor drones where lift force scales with mass.

Speed Ratio Gate for Drone Viability.definition: Pre-filter candidate drone-assisted deliveries: only consider drone use when drone speed is at least twice the truck speed, as lower ratios yield negligible time savings after synchronization overhead.
Speed Ratio Gate for Drone Viability.condition: When deciding whether to include drone operations in route planning; based on empirical evidence that drone speed < 2× truck undermines makespan gains.

Mobile Depot Recharging Synchronization.definition: Enforce that a drone must rendezvous with a mobile depot (truck) not only for launch/recovery but also for battery recharging, requiring both temporal synchronization and energy balance updates when docked.
Mobile Depot Recharging Synchronization.condition: When a ground vehicle acts as a mobile charging station for drones, enabling mid-route battery replenishment, and drone sorties depend on recharging opportunities that occur only at rendezvous points along the truck's route.

Energy-Balance Routing with Recharging S.definition: Extend the vehicle routing network with charging/swapping station nodes, track state of charge via continuous variables at each visited node, and enforce energy balance and reset only when a charging node is visited.
Energy-Balance Routing with Recharging S.condition: When battery‑powered drones have limited endurance and recharging/swapping infrastructure exists at discrete locations, requiring mid‑route energy replenishment.

Coverage Pattern Orientation Based on Mi.definition: Align the back-and-forth lawnmower tracks to be parallel to the region's minimum convex width direction to minimize the number of 180° turns required by the vehicle's minimum turn radius.
Coverage Pattern Orientation Based on Mi.condition: Applies when planning area coverage paths for vehicles with a Dubins (minimum turn radius) constraint; exclude if turns have negligible cost or the region is not convex.

Signal-Shadowed Arc Penalty.definition: Add a cost penalty per unit distance on arcs that traverse zones with high building density causing poor SINR, to route vehicles away from communication‑dead spots.
Signal-Shadowed Arc Penalty.condition: When a UAV requires reliable datalink and terrain/building databases provide expected SINR. Penalize arcs where SINR falls below a threshold; exclude if communication is not flight‑critical.

Coverage Overlap Constraint for Minimum.definition: For parallel flight passes in a back-and-forth coverage pattern, enforce that the pass spacing d satisfies d ≤ W − 2R_min to prevent uncovered strips caused by the vehicle's minimum turn radius R_min, where W is the effective swath width.
Coverage Overlap Constraint for Minimum.condition: When planning area coverage paths for a fixed-wing UAV with minimum turn radius and finite swath width; exclude if the vehicle can hover or has zero turn radius (multirotor).

Time-Space Discretization Recharging VRP.definition: Discretize the planning horizon into time slots and the service area into spatial cells; model each feasible recharging operation as a set of (charger, time‑slot, location) that a drone must select, reducing synchronization to a set‑partitioning problem.
Time-Space Discretization Recharging VRP.condition: When recharging stations are mobile (e.g., ground robots) and recharging must occur within specific time windows. Exclude if recharging is at fixed static depots with no temporal synchronization or if the number of charge events is small enough to schedule continuously.

Wind-Vector Energy Consumption Model.definition: Incorporate the effect of wind speed and direction on drone energy consumption per flight segment using a function of ground speed derived from the wind vector, typically approximated piecewise‑linearly for MILP.
Wind-Vector Energy Consumption Model.condition: When drones fly outdoors where wind significantly alters range, and energy constraints must be accurate. Exclude calm‑weather operations or when a simple distance‑proportional model is adequate.

Single-Package-per-Sortie Payload Simpli.definition: When each drone flight carries at most one package, the payload constraint reduces to at most one delivery per sortie, eliminating the need for multi‑drop weight tracking and converting the routing to a set‑partitioning problem.
Single-Package-per-Sortie Payload Simpli.condition: Applies when drone payload capacity is exactly one standard package (or all packages are identical units). Exclude when drones carry multiple heterogeneous items requiring knapsack packing or weight‑dependent energy consumption per segment.

Neighborhood One-per-Region Coverage Con.definition: For each coverage region, exactly one candidate point must be visited; ∑_{p∈region} v_p = 1, where v_p indicates point p is visited. This converts area coverage into a routing problem with discrete representative points.
Neighborhood One-per-Region Coverage Con.condition: Applies when each region's sensor footprint or data collection requirement can be satisfied by visiting any one of several candidate points within that region; exclude if coverage requires area sweeping or continuous sensing.

Turn-Cost Sequence Dependency.definition: Add a turn penalty cost c(i,j,k) that depends on the preceding edge (k,i) due to the vehicle’s minimum turn radius (Dubins). This makes the TSP cost sequence‑dependent (k‑neighbor TSP).
Turn-Cost Sequence Dependency.condition: When UAV routes must respect a minimum turn radius and turning is costly in time/energy; exclude if turn cost is negligible or can be approximated by adding extra straight‑line distance.

Terrain-Elevation Energy Multiplier.definition: Incorporate altitude change Δh along an arc into energy consumption via a factor f(Δh), e.g., E = d·(base + k_climb·max(0,Δh) + k_descend·|min(0,Δh)|).
Terrain-Elevation Energy Multiplier.condition: When UAV routes traverse terrain with significant elevation variation; exclude over flat terrain where altitude change is negligible.

Processing-Time Dominance Routing Simpli.definition: When service/handling times far exceed inter-stop travel times, routing reduces to scheduling with negligible travel.
Processing-Time Dominance Routing Simpli.condition: Processing (charging, unloading, sensing) time per stop ≥ 10× the flight time between stops, so travel sequencing has negligible impact on objective.

Safe-Node Drone Recovery Restriction.definition: Only allow drone launch or recovery at truck stops that are designated as safe parking nodes; enforce by pre‑filtering drone sortie variables or adding constraints linking drone sortie to truck stop safety attribute.
Safe-Node Drone Recovery Restriction.condition: When a drone must land on a truck parked at a safe node (e.g., cleared area, good visibility); exclude if the truck can recover drones while moving or any generic stop works.

Cellular Decomposition for Coverage Path.definition: Divide a non-convex coverage region into non-overlapping convex cells via exact cellular decomposition, plan back-and-forth (Boustrophedon) tracks within each cell, solve a sequencing problem (TSP) over cell entry/exit points, and apply turn-radius smoothing to produce a continuous coverage path.
Cellular Decomposition for Coverage Path.condition: When the coverage area contains obstacles or concavities that prevent a single continuous back-and-forth pattern, and the UAV has a minimum turn radius; excludes simple convex regions where a single pattern suffices.

Connectivity Feasibility Mask.definition: Allow a UAV to traverse only waypoints or arcs that are within communication range and line-of-sight of at least one active ground station or relay; implemented by pre-computing a binary mask from a communication coverage map and excluding infeasible waypoints from the routing network.
Connectivity Feasibility Mask.condition: When the UAV must maintain real-time command or data link and coverage is static; exclude if dynamic communication models require detailed SINR constraints embedded in routing.

Coverage Quality Hard Constraint.definition: Route must visit each target at a point where sensor detection accuracy meets a minimum threshold; feasible inspection points are precomputed as those where accuracy ≥ threshold, then each target must be assigned at least one such point in the route.
Coverage Quality Hard Constraint.condition: When inspection missions (e.g., PV panels, infrastructure) require a guaranteed detection accuracy per target, and accuracy depends on distance, angle, or altitude. Exclude if accuracy is constant or only soft targets.

Speed-Payload Energy Consumption Constra.definition: Energy consumed along an arc is a function of both speed and payload weight, typically modeled as e = distance·f(speed, payload) where f is piecewise linear. Different power sources (battery, hydrogen) have distinct parameter sets.
Speed-Payload Energy Consumption Constra.condition: When drone power draw varies with flight speed (e.g., aerodynamic drag) and payload mass, and energy constraints must be tight; exclude when speed is fixed or payload is negligible.

Time-Indexed Variables.definition: Binary x_{j,t} = 1 if job j starts or runs at time t.
Time-Indexed Variables.condition: Applies when the problem description requires modeling job starts or executions period by period.

Precedence Constraints.definition: Job A must finish before job B starts: start_B ≥ finish_A + lag.
Precedence Constraints.condition: Applies when the problem domain contains tasks with technological or logical order requirements.

Resource-Leveling Constraints.definition: Smooth resource usage across periods using capacity limits.
Resource-Leveling Constraints.condition: Applies when the problem description requires balancing workload across periods to reduce peaks while meeting deadlines.

Disjunctive Temporal Separation Constrai.definition: For each pair of flights using a shared corridor, enforce a minimum time gap via binary order variable and Big‑M.
Disjunctive Temporal Separation Constrai.condition: When vehicles share a one‑way segment and must maintain a minimum time headway to avoid conflicts; continuous‑time scheduling.

Resource-Constrained Turnaround Scheduli.definition: A vehicle arriving at a vertiport requires a sequence of ground tasks (charging, MRO, passenger handling) with fixed durations and specific resource needs; tasks must be scheduled respecting precedence and finite resource capacities to release the vehicle for its next departure.
Resource-Constrained Turnaround Scheduli.condition: When vertiport ground operations involve limited, shared resources (chargers, maintenance bays, gates) and turnaround time directly affects throughput.

Resource-Driven Deadline Constraint.definition: Impose a hard deadline t_complete ≤ t_current + (remaining_resource − safety_reserve) / resource_depletion_rate, derived from a depletable resource like battery energy.
Resource-Driven Deadline Constraint.condition: When a depletable resource limits available operation time, and the resource depletes at a known average rate; missing the deadline would exhaust the resource before tasks finish, requiring priority-based reordering.

Sequence-Dependent Separation Times.definition: When two flights use the same resource (pad, corridor), the minimum time gap between them depends on the ordered pair of flight types, modeled via a setup-time matrix used in disjunctive constraints.
Sequence-Dependent Separation Times.condition: Applies when flights are heterogeneous (different wake categories, D‑values) and the required spatial or temporal separation is a function of the leading and following vehicle types, not a constant.
Sequence-Dependent Separation Times.explanation: Use binary ordering variables y_{i,j}=1 if flight i precedes j on the resource. Enforce start_j ≥ finish_i + setup_{type_i, type_j} − M(1−y_{i,j}), where setup is a precomputed matrix of required gaps. This transforms arrival scheduling into a single‑machine problem with sequence‑dependent setups, allowing accurate wake/ separation compliance.
Sequence-Dependent Separation Times.example: Given two flight types A (small) and B (large), setup_{A,B}=45 s, setup_{B,A}=60 s. For flights i and j assigned to the same pad, add constraints: start_j ≥ end_i + 45 − M(1−y_{ij}) and start_i ≥ end_j + 60 − M y_{ij}.

Simultaneous Resource Exclusion (Spatial.definition: For any pair of pads that cannot be occupied simultaneously due to wake turbulence, shared taxiway, or spatial overlap, enforce that at most one of them operates at any time via a constraint x_i + x_j ≤ 1.
Simultaneous Resource Exclusion (Spatial.condition: When pads are not independent and shared ground infrastructure or safety zone overlaps prevent concurrent use, leading to dependency.

Fixed Incumbent Occupancy Forbidden Inte.definition: When a resource is already partially occupied by a legacy schedule (incumbent users) that cannot be modified, new operations must avoid those pre‑booked time intervals.
Fixed Incumbent Occupancy Forbidden Inte.condition: Applies when a new operational mode (e.g., UAM) must share physical infrastructure (gates/stands) with an incumbent mode (conventional jets) whose schedule is fixed and non‑negotiable.

Charging Schedule Grid Limit.definition: Enforce that the total electrical load from all vehicles charging simultaneously at a facility does not exceed the facility's grid connection capacity during any time interval.
Charging Schedule Grid Limit.condition: Applies when eVTOL scheduling includes charging periods and the vertiport has a limited electrical supply that must not be exceeded at any time.

Indicator-Enforced Time Windows.definition: Use indicator constraints (if x=1 then t ∈ [a,b]) to enforce time windows conditional on assignment, avoiding Big‑M instability.
Indicator-Enforced Time Windows.condition: When a time window must be respected only if a task is assigned to a resource; the assignment variable is binary.

Lagrangian Precedence Relaxation (Smith'.definition: In single‑machine scheduling with precedence constraints and weighted completion time objective, dualize the precedence constraints to obtain a subproblem that minimizes the weighted sum of completion times subject to release dates only; this subproblem is solved by the WSPT (Smith's) rule, providing a lower bound.
Lagrangian Precedence Relaxation (Smith'.condition: Applies when sequencing jobs (UAV tasks, flights) on a single resource with known release dates, processing times, weights, and precedence requirements that complicate the schedule; relaxing precedence yields a tractable greedy solution.

Cumulative Resource Capacity Constraints.definition: Sum of resource demands of all jobs active at time t must not exceed capacity C, repeated for all t.
Cumulative Resource Capacity Constraints.condition: When tasks consume a limited shared resource over time and may overlap. Applies to airspace sector capacity, processor time, charging slots; excludes if tasks are non-overlapping or have infinite capacity.

Attention Budget with Rest Replenishment.definition: Track operator attention as a depletable resource that decreases while supervising UAVs and replenishes only during mandated rest breaks, with hard upper bound on continuous attention and penalty for exceeding soft limits.
Attention Budget with Rest Replenishment.condition: When an operator monitors multiple UAVs and workload regulations impose maximum continuous time on task followed by a mandatory inactive period. Exclude when monitoring is fully automated.

Coverage Handover Continuity Constraint.definition: For persistent monitoring with finite-endurance drones, enforce temporal overlap between consecutive sorties at the same coverage point.
Coverage Handover Continuity Constraint.condition: Multiple drones must provide uninterrupted sensor coverage, and each sortie has a maximum duration due to battery with required handover time.

Cognitive Load Alternation Constraint.definition: Limit the number of consecutive high‑demand tasks assigned to a human operator and enforce a minimum gap of low‑load tasks after such bursts, typically using sequence‑based counting or penalty terms.
Cognitive Load Alternation Constraint.condition: When an operator monitors UAVs carrying out tasks of varying cognitive difficulty and sustained high load degrades performance; exclude if all tasks have uniform demand or operator rest is not modeled.

Endogenous SoC-Driven Setup Times.definition: The minimum time gap between consecutive uses of a resource (pad, charger) depends on the arriving vehicle's battery state of charge (SoC), which is itself an outcome of the prior flight's energy consumption and routing decisions.
Endogenous SoC-Driven Setup Times.condition: When turnaround/charging duration is not a fixed parameter but a function of how much energy the vehicle expended on its inbound leg, coupling routing energy balance with ground scheduling sequence-dependent setups.

Threshold-Triggered Priority Override.definition: When a flight's remaining endurance or accumulated delay exceeds a critical threshold, its priority overrides FCFS ordering, enforced via binary critical-state variables and precedence constraints.
Threshold-Triggered Priority Override.condition: Applies when FCFS scheduling is standard but under certain critical conditions (low endurance, high delay) the order must be violated to preserve feasibility or service level.

Alternative Service Mode Selection (Char.definition: A vehicle at a gate can select one of multiple service processes (e.g., battery charging or swapping) that differ in duration and resource requirements; expressed via binary variables and constraints linking turnaround time to the selected mode.
Alternative Service Mode Selection (Char.condition: Applies when a vehicle requires ground service that can be performed in mutually exclusive ways, with at least one mode’s duration dependent on the vehicle’s state-of-charge (SoC) and another’s duration fixed but may require special infrastructure.

Inventory Balance Equations.definition: Same as production but may include safety stock or backlog.
Inventory Balance Equations.condition: Applies when the problem domain involves inventory evolving over time with safety stock or backlog policies.

Multi Period Resource Balance.definition: Ensure cumulative inflow ≥ cumulative demand across horizon.
Multi Period Resource Balance.condition: Applies when the problem description requires cumulative feasibility across multiple periods instead of per-period checks.

Network‑Flow Reformulation for Integrali.definition: Reformulate multi‑period inventory balances as a minimum‑cost network flow; the node‑arc incidence matrix is totally unimodular, so continuous flows give integer solutions when supplies/demands are integer.
Network‑Flow Reformulation for Integrali.condition: When inventory/production costs are linear, there are no fixed charges, and demands are integer.

Binary Selection Constraints.definition: Pick subset of items with 0-1 variables and cardinality limit.
Binary Selection Constraints.condition: Applies when the problem domain requires choosing a subset under count, budget, or compatibility limits.

Submodular Greedy Maximization.definition: Select a subset of items to maximize a monotone submodular set function subject to a cardinality or matroid constraint; a greedy algorithm that iteratively adds the item with largest marginal gain yields a (1-1/e) approximation to the optimum.
Submodular Greedy Maximization.condition: When the objective function exhibits diminishing returns (submodularity) and is monotone non‑decreasing, and the constraint is a cardinality limit or matroid (e.g., budget on number of facilities).

Matroid Greedy Optimality.definition: When the feasible subsets of items form a matroid, the greedy algorithm (iteratively add highest‑weight element that maintains independence) yields an optimal maximum‑weight independent set.
Matroid Greedy Optimality.condition: When selecting a subset under independence constraints that satisfy matroid axioms (hereditary, augmentation); objective is linear weight maximization. Exclude when constraints violate matroid properties (e.g., knapsack capacity).

Load Balancing Constraints.definition: Keep workload across agents within a tolerance band.
Load Balancing Constraints.condition: Applies when the problem description requires fairness or controls maximum imbalance across parallel resources.

Time-Order Fairness Constraints.definition: Limit the deviation of the scheduled sequence from a reference (often first‑come‑first‑served) order, measured per operator, via absolute or quadratic deviation penalties, or a maximum number of overtakes per operator.
Time-Order Fairness Constraints.condition: When multiple operators share a resource and fairness is defined as preserving or minimally disturbing the original request order for each operator, avoiding systematic discrimination.
Time-Order Fairness Constraints.explanation: Assign each flight a reference position r_i (arrival order). In the scheduling model, compute scheduled position s_i (or schedule time) for each flight. Fairness can be enforced by capping |s_i − r_i| per operator, minimizing ∑_i w_op(i) * max(0, r_i − s_i) to penalize overtakes, or constraining the number of reversals among flights of the same operator.
Time-Order Fairness Constraints.example: For operator op, let flts_op be its flights sorted by earliest requested arrival. In scheduling, for any pair (i,j) where i is earlier in the request order, penalize violation if j scheduled before i by weight w_op, or add constraint: if i precedes j in request order, then s_i ≤ s_j + BigM * (1 − z_{op}) where z_{op} limits overtaking allowance.

Min-Max Workload Deviation.definition: Define minimum and maximum total workload across agents using solver general constraints (min/max), then penalize the spread (max − min).
Min-Max Workload Deviation.condition: When workloads are accumulated via sums of assignments, fairness requires limiting the range of individual workloads, and the number of agents is moderate enough to use min/max functions.

Knapsack Constraints.definition: Capacity ∑ w_i x_i ≤ C with binary x_i selecting items.
Knapsack Constraints.condition: Applies when the problem domain requires selecting items that consume a single scalar capacity such as weight, volume, or budget.

Incompatible Items Splitting Constraint.definition: Prohibit co‑transportation of items that are mutually incompatible (e.g., hot and cold meals, hazardous and non‑hazardous) in the same vehicle, container, or compartment.
Incompatible Items Splitting Constraint.condition: When transported items have compatibility restrictions that forbid certain pairs from sharing a vehicle or container; triggers order splitting across drones or compartments.

Scenario-Contingent Demand.definition: Represent uncertain demand as a finite set of discrete scenarios with associated probabilities, and optimize expected performance or worst-case cost across scenarios.
Scenario-Contingent Demand.condition: Applies when demand parameters are random and can be captured by a limited number of plausible realizations derived from forecasts.

Linear Degradation with Partial Reset.definition: A resource degrades linearly over time; imperfect rejuvenation partially restores it with known downtime; degradation rate is uncertain, modeled via discrete scenarios.
Linear Degradation with Partial Reset.condition: When a system or component accumulates wear at an uncertain rate and can be partially reset through maintenance that incurs a fixed downtime cost.

Chance-Constrained Weather Feasibility.definition: Transform a wind operational limit (e.g., crosswind ≤ 10.5 kts) into a chance constraint that the exceedance probability is ≤ ε, using historical wind data to precompute feasibility for each candidate orientation.
Chance-Constrained Weather Feasibility.condition: When siting infrastructure that is sensitive to wind direction/speed (e.g., vertiport pads) and long-term METAR records are available.

Preemptive Buffer Reservation under Stoc.definition: First stage reserves buffer capacity (pads, chargers) at selected bases; second stage assigns stochastic high-priority demand (medevac) to buffers, with unmet demand penalized heavily. Regular throughput is reduced by the reserved buffer.
Preemptive Buffer Reservation under Stoc.condition: When high-priority missions (medevac, emergency) arrive stochastically and must preempt scheduled operations, requiring dedicated reserve capacity sized in the investment stage before demand realizations are known.
